paragraphs.heading: What titration is
paragraphs.text: Titration, also called titrimetry or volumetric analysis, is a common lab method for finding the concentration of a known substance in a sample. That substance is the analyte, meaning the thing being analysed. A second solution, the titrant, is made up beforehand with a known concentration and volume. The titrant reacts with the analyte, and the amount of titrant used up, called the titration volume, reveals how concentrated the analyte was.

paragraphs.heading: How it is done
paragraphs.text: A flask or beaker holds a carefully measured amount of analyte plus a little indicator, such as phenolphthalein. Above it sits a calibrated burette or syringe filled with titrant. Small portions of titrant go in until the indicator changes color, which marks the endpoint, where the titrant has balanced the analyte. Close to the end, a single drop or even less can decide whether the color change lasts or fades. The flask is kept stirred so the added titrant spreads evenly.

paragraphs.heading: Practical adjustments
paragraphs.text: Both titrant and analyte are normally liquids, so solids are usually dissolved in water first, while solvents such as ethanol or glacial acetic acid serve special uses. Concentrated samples are often diluted to make the result more accurate. Many titrations that are not acid–base reactions need a steady pH, so a buffer solution may be added to hold it. When a second substance would also react with the titrant, a masking solution can cancel its effect. Some redox titrations are done while the sample is still hot, to speed the reaction up; certain oxalate solutions are heated to 60 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a titration curve
paragraphs.text: A titration curve plots the volume of titrant added along the bottom against the analyte's concentration up the side, which in an acid–base titration is usually shown as pH. Its key landmark is the equivalence point, which is set by the proportions in the balanced reaction. For a strong acid with a strong base, the curve turns very steep near that point, so a tiny extra volume makes the pH leap and many indicators will do. If one side is weak and the other strong, the curve is irregular and the pH moves less near the equivalence point. With a weak acid and a weak base the curve is so irregular that no single indicator may suit, and a pH meter often tracks the reaction instead.

paragraphs.heading: Picking the right indicator
paragraphs.text: The endpoint and the equivalence point are not quite the same thing, because the endpoint is simply when the indicator changes color. Choosing the indicator with care cuts down the indicator error. If the equivalence point sits at pH 8.4, for example, phenolphthalein is a better choice than Alizarin Yellow. When oxalic acid, a weak acid, is titrated with sodium hydroxide, a strong base, the equivalence point falls between pH 8 and 10, so the mixture is basic there and phenolphthalein fits.

paragraphs.heading: From gold coins to glassware
paragraphs.text: The word goes back to the French tiltre of 1543, the share of gold or silver in a coin, a gauge of its purity. It became titre, then came to mean how concentrated a substance is in a sample, and in 1828 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac first used it as a verb. The first burette was built by François-Antoine-Henri Descroizilles in 1791, and Gay-Lussac coined the words pipette and burette in 1824. Karl Friedrich Mohr later gave the burette a simple, handy shape and in 1855 published the first textbook on the method.
